prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: [val] עברית · שורות מתויגות (language he, right-to-left: column 1 is on the RIGHT).
Grid: 4 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "נושא" · longest unbreakable word 56px · one-line width 136px
  col 2: header "אחראי" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 38px
  col 3: header "סטטוס" · longest unbreakable word 43px · one-line width 43px
  col 4: header "הערות" · longest unbreakable word 50px · one-line width 315px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 433px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 432px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"good","why":"The row labels and short status columns are easy to scan, though the first label wraps and the notes need three lines."},"B":{"grade":"poor","why":"The owner column has surplus space while the notes and row labels wrap heavily, making the rows tall and uneven."},"C":{"grade":"excellent","why":"All row labels stay on one line, the owner and status columns remain compact, and the notes wrap without disrupting row comparison."},"D":{"grade":"good","why":"The wider notes column keeps notes to two lines, but all three row labels wrap, weakening the right-hand scanning edge."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"Notes fit comfortably in two lines and the short columns are compact, though every row label wraps."},"F":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"The notes have ample room, but the narrow row-header column breaks one label across three lines and makes the table less balanced."}},"best":["C"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"The choice between C and the wider notes in D or E depends on how much priority readers give to scanning row labels versus reading notes."}
